source.name: FAA PHAK, Chapter 14, p. 14-8
source.rightsNote: Original educational adaptation; the source citation is retained from the legacy article bank.

paragraphs.en: Runway numbers help pilots identify the direction in which a runway is aligned. The number generally corresponds to its magnetic direction rounded to the nearest ten degrees, with the final zero omitted. For example, a runway aligned near 090 degrees may be labeled Runway 09.

Because the same pavement can be used in opposite directions, the runway numbers at its two ends are normally eighteen numbers apart. A runway labeled 09 at one end is generally labeled 27 at the other. Airports with parallel runways use letters such as L, C, and R to distinguish left, center, and right.

Runway designations can change when the local magnetic reference changes sufficiently over time. Pilots must therefore use current airport information rather than assuming that a runway will keep the same number forever.
Understanding runway numbering helps crews interpret clearances and charts, but the designation alone does not describe the airport's complete departure or approach procedures.
